rationale: The unit opens on the vocative "בְּ֭נִי" (oshb:Prov.5.1) paired with the imperative “pay attention” (web:Prov.5.1), the address-formula that restarts the lecture cycle after 4:27. The six verses run a single argument: attention to wisdom (5:1-2) guards against a seductress whose speech is honeyed but whose end is bitter (5:3-4), whose path runs to death (5:5), and who gives no thought to the "אֹ֣רַח חַ֭יִּים" (oshb:Prov.5.6; “way of life”, web:Prov.5.6) she cannot see. The closing clause of 5:6 answers the opening appeal to wisdom with its negative — she lacks the very discernment 5:1-2 commends — which closes the argument before 5:7 restarts the address with a plural vocative.
rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through 5:14 to absorb the following appeal was rejected because 5:7 opens a fresh imperative summons on a different vocative form rather than continuing the invitation begun at 5:1.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Prov.5.1 vocative "בְּ֭נִי" + imperative verse-initial
oshb:Prov.5.3-5.4 honey/oil vs wormwood/edges antithetic pivot
oshb:Prov.5.5 feet-to-death, Sheol motion verbs
oshb:Prov.5.6 closing clause "אֹ֣רַח חַ֭יִּים" negated
device_notes: Synthetic parallelism across the span (its lines elaborate rather than negate their neighbors), with one antithetic-shaped contrast internal to 5:3-4 (“smoother than oil, but in the end...”, web:Prov.5.4) that does not by itself split the unit. A petuchah closes oshb:Prov.5.6 in the Leningrad tradition (tier-3 corroboration, single witness); it is consistent with, not the basis of, the boundary argued above. Hazard note: 5:4 “two-edged sword” (web:Prov.5.4) renders "כְּחֶ֣רֶב פִּיּֽוֹת" (oshb:Prov.5.4, "sword of edges") — the "two" is a WEB rendering choice, not a Hebrew numeral, so no numerical claim is made from this verse.

rationale: A new address opens the unit: "וְעַתָּ֣ה בָ֭נִים שִׁמְעוּ" (oshb:Prov.5.7; “Now therefore, my sons, listen to me”, web:Prov.5.7), a plural vocative distinct from the singular "my son" of 5:1, marked by the inferential particle that signals a discourse restart rather than a continuation. The imperatives of 5:8 (keep your way far from her, do not approach her door) and the motive clauses of 5:9-11 build toward a first-person quoted lament (5:12-14) in which the addressee, cast forward as having ignored the warning, confesses hatred of instruction and near-ruin “among the gathered assembly” (web:Prov.5.14). That quoted confession closes the argument; 5:15 opens a new positive exhortation on a different subject (the addressee's own wife) with a fresh imperative.
rejected_alternative: Reading 5:7-14 as part of one chapter-spanning lecture was rejected because the imperative-warning register of 5:7-14 gives way at 5:15 to affirmative marital counsel built on an unrelated image set (cistern, spring, doe).
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Prov.5.7 plural vocative "וְעַתָּ֣ה בָ֭נִים שִׁמְעוּ" reopening address
oshb:Prov.5.8 imperative prohibition (keep-far / do-not-approach pair)
oshb:Prov.5.9-5.11 pen-clause consequence chain (lest-clauses)
oshb:Prov.5.12-5.14 first-person quoted confession, verb of regret
device_notes: Synthetic/consequential parallelism (cause then result across couplets), no antithetic "but" pivot within the span. A petuchah closes the preceding verse, oshb:Prov.5.6 (tier-3 corroboration, single witness), at the seam just before this unit opens; the parashah layer is otherwise silent across 5:7-14, so the address-formula and mood shift argued above, not parashah corroboration, carry this internal seam.

rationale: The imperative "שְׁתֵה מַ֥יִם" (oshb:Prov.5.15; “Drink water”, web:Prov.5.15) opens a positive counterpart to the preceding warning: instead of the stranger's door (5:8), the addressee is directed to his own cistern, well, and spring (5:15-17), then to bless that spring and “Rejoice in the wife of your youth” (web:Prov.5.18), closing with the doe/deer figure of 5:19. The unit is bounded by a change of addressee-object (from the adulteress to the wife) and grammatical mood (from prohibition to affirmative imperative and blessing), and closes before 5:20 pivots back to an interrogative warning.
rejected_alternative: Folding 5:15-19 into the unit that follows was rejected because 5:20 shifts from affirmative imperative and blessing to an interrogative warning, a distinct rhetorical mode addressed to a different object.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Prov.5.15 imperative verse-initial "שְׁתֵה מַ֥יִם"
oshb:Prov.5.16-5.17 cistern/spring/well image chain, second person
oshb:Prov.5.18 blessing formula + "wife of your youth"
oshb:Prov.5.19 doe/deer figure closing the image chain
device_notes: Synthetic parallelism (image built across five verses), not antithetic. No petuchah falls inside 5:15-19; the preceding unit's petuchah (5:6) and the chapter-closing one (5:23) bracket this span without marking it directly, so the seam rests on the imagery and mood shift argued above.

rationale: The rhetorical question "וְלָ֤מָּה תִשְׁגֶּ֣ה בְנִ֣י..." (oshb:Prov.5.20; “why should you, my son, be captivated...”, web:Prov.5.20) reopens direct address with the vocative recurring as the third word of the verse (not verse-initial, unlike the unit-opening occurrences at 5:1 and 6:1). The unit moves from the question (5:20) to a Yahweh-observation clause (5:21, “the ways of man are before Yahweh's eyes”, web:Prov.5.21) to the wicked man's self-entrapment by his own iniquities (5:22) and his death for lack of instruction (5:23), one question-to-consequence argument that the petuchah at oshb:Prov.5.23 marks off as its own unit.
rejected_alternative: Isolating 5:21 as its own one-verse row for its Yahweh-clause was rejected because the argument needs the self-entrapment and death clauses of 5:22-23 to complete, clauses that the petuchah at oshb:Prov.5.23 closes.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Prov.5.20 mid-verse vocative "וְלָ֤מָּה תִשְׁגֶּ֣ה בְנִ֣י"
oshb:Prov.5.21 YHWH-eyes clause, exact token יהוה
oshb:Prov.5.22 self-entrapment figure (cords/snare of his own sin)
oshb:Prov.5.23 death-for-lack-of-instruction closing clause
device_notes: The vocative here is not verse-initial and stands apart from the book's early-chapter lecture-opening occurrences of "my son"; it is disclosed here as a distinct mid-verse recurrence, not counted against that set. Synthetic parallelism (the verses advance the consequence chain in sequence); no antithetic pivot. A petuchah closes oshb:Prov.5.23 in the Leningrad tradition (tier-3 corroboration, single witness), consistent with the chapter boundary; it does not by itself argue the internal 5:20 seam.

rationale: "בְּ֭נִי אִם עָרַ֣בְתָּ..." (oshb:Prov.6.1; “My son, if you have become collateral...”, web:Prov.6.1) opens a self-contained admonition on suretyship: a conditional protasis (6:1) is answered by a diagnosis of self-entrapment (6:2), an urgent remedy in triple imperative (6:3, "do this... humble yourself... press your plea"), and a further pair of imperatives against sleep until the addressee is free like "כִּצְבִ֣י" (oshb:Prov.6.5, "a gazelle") “from the hand of the hunter” (web:Prov.6.5). The topic (a pledge for a neighbor) and the closing simile pair are confined to these five verses; 6:6 opens an unrelated imperative address to an unnamed sluggard.
rejected_alternative: Merging 6:1-5 with the material that follows was rejected because 6:6 opens a fresh imperative on a wholly different addressee-type (an unnamed sluggard) rather than continuing the surety scenario.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Prov.6.1 vocative "בְּ֭נִי אִם עָרַ֣בְתָּ" + conditional protasis
oshb:Prov.6.2 diagnosis, self-snaring by own words
oshb:Prov.6.3 triple imperative remedy sequence
oshb:Prov.6.5 simile pair, "כִּצְבִ֣י" (gazelle) / bird from the fowler's snare
device_notes: Synthetic parallelism (condition, diagnosis, remedy in sequence); the gazelle/bird simile pair in 6:5 is this unit's explicit figure of comparison. A petuchah closes oshb:Prov.6.5 in WLC (tier-3 corroboration, single witness), matching the boundary argued from the topic and address shift at 6:6. The verse immediately before this unit, oshb:Prov.5.23, closes with its own petuchah in WLC (tier-3 corroboration, single witness), marking the end of the preceding chapter; disclosed here as the span-adjacent mark, it does not bear on the 6:1 opening argued above. A paseq seg is attested at 6:3; the inventory is a presence tally, not a position record, so no intra-verse placement is claimed here.

rationale: "לֵֽךְ אֶל נְמָלָ֥ה עָצֵ֑ל..." (oshb:Prov.6.6; “Go to the ant, you sluggard”, web:Prov.6.6) opens a second-person imperative address built on an observed-nature example: the ant's self-directed provision without overseer (6.7-8) is set against a rhetorical question to the sluggard (“How long will you sleep...”, web:Prov.6.9) and a mimicked quotation of his own procrastination (6:10), closing with the consequence of poverty arriving “as a robber” (web:Prov.6.11). The governing verbs stay second-person imperative and interrogative across the unit, distinct from the third-person participial portrait that opens at 6:12.
rejected_alternative: Classing 6:6-11 with the book's named wisdom_poem spans (1:20-33; ch 8; ch 9) was rejected because it is governed by direct second-person imperative and interrogative address to a sluggard, not the third-person hymnic voice that marks those poems.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Prov.6.6 imperative verse-initial "לֵֽךְ אֶל נְמָלָ֥ה עָצֵ֑ל"

oshb:Prov.6.10-6.11 mimicked quotation + robber/armed-man consequence pair
device_notes: Synthetic build (example, question, mimicry, consequence); no antithetic pivot. A petuchah closes oshb:Prov.6.11 in WLC (tier-3, single-witness corroboration), aligning with the topic shift to the worthless-person portrait at 6:12. oshb:Prov.6.5, the verse just before this unit, is itself petuchah-closed in WLC (tier-3, single-witness corroboration); disclosed as the adjoining mark, distinct from the 6:11 boundary argued above. Paseq segs fall at 6:9 and 6:10; the inventory tallies their presence without recording position, so no intra-verse placement is claimed for either.

rationale: The span opens with a nominal characterization, "אָדָ֣ם בְּ֭לִיַּעַל אִ֣ישׁ אָ֑וֶן" (oshb:Prov.6.12; “A worthless person, a man of iniquity”, web:Prov.6.12), and continues as a chain of participial clauses sharing that one grammatical subject: a perverse mouth (6.12), winking eyes / signaling feet / motioning fingers (6.13), and a scheming heart (6.14) — a cumulative character portrait rather than direct address or imperative instruction. The chain closes when "עַל כֵּ֗ן" (oshb:Prov.6.15; “therefore”, web:Prov.6.15) draws the causal consequence (sudden, remedyless calamity) from the accumulated portrait, tying 6:15 back to the subject introduced in 6:12 and closing the unit before the numerical formula of 6:16 opens a new list-governed unit.
rejected_alternative: Treating 6:12-15 as an admonition_unit was rejected because its verbs are third-person participles describing a character type rather than second-person imperatives addressed to the reader; the cohesion is a shared grammatical subject carried across four verses, not a single couplet, so single_proverb was also rejected.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Prov.6.12 nominal-subject opener "אָדָ֣ם בְּ֭לִיַּעַל אִ֣ישׁ אָ֑וֶן"
oshb:Prov.6.13 three-part participial body-part chain (eyes/feet/fingers)

device_notes: Synthetic, cumulative parallelism (portrait building toward one consequence), not antithetic. A petuchah closes oshb:Prov.6.15 in WLC (tier-3, single-witness), consistent with the boundary argued from the causal clause. A petuchah is also attested one verse earlier, at oshb:Prov.6.11 (tier-3 corroboration, single witness), closing the sluggard unit that precedes this span; it is disclosed here as the adjoining mark rather than as evidence for the 6:12 opening argued above. A ketiv/qere note attaches to 6:14 (oshb:Prov.6.14: ketiv "מדנים", plural spelling, against qere "מִדְיָנִ֥ים") — disclosed here because the span touches it; the note affects the spelling of "discord," not the boundary. A paseq seg is also attested at 6:14; the inventory marks presence, not position, so no intra-verse placement is claimed here either.

rationale: "שֶׁשׁ הֵ֭נָּה... וְ֝שֶׁ֗בַע" (oshb:Prov.6.16; “six things... yes, seven”, web:Prov.6.16) opens an x-of-y numerical formula whose count (6.16) is answered by exactly seven enumerated items across 6:17-19 (arrogant eyes, lying tongue, bloodshedding hands, a scheming heart, feet swift to evil, a false witness, and one who sows discord among brothers). The unit is chunked by that count-to-list function rather than split mid-enumeration: the formula opened in 6:16 completes with the seventh item at 6:19, not any earlier. (A ketiv/qere pair also sits in 6:16, disclosed in the signals and notes below; it bears on the noun's number/state, not on the count.)
rejected_alternative: Splitting the count-verse (6:16) from its seven-item list (6:17-19) into separate rows was rejected because the x-of-y formula is one function unit: the count and its enumeration complete together, not apart.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Prov.6.16 numeral pair "שֶׁשׁ הֵ֭נָּה...וְ֝שֶׁ֗בַע" (six...seven); the same verse carries a ketiv/qere pair (see next signal), disclosed here rather than treated as a driver

oshb:Prov.6.17-6.19 seven-item enumerated list, body-part + abstract-vice pairing
device_notes: List-register unit, chunked by function per the numerical-saying rule rather than by verse-count target. A petuchah closes oshb:Prov.6.19 in WLC (tier-3 corroboration, single witness). The verse preceding this span, oshb:Prov.6.15, likewise closes with a petuchah in WLC (tier-3, single-witness); disclosed here as the adjoining mark, it does not argue the 6:16 numerical-formula opening. The ketiv/qere note at 6:16 concerns the noun's number/state (plural ketiv vs construct-singular qere), not the count "seven."

rationale: "נְצֹ֣ר בְּ֭נִי מִצְוַ֣ת אָבִ֑יךָ..." (oshb:Prov.6.20; “My son, keep your father's commandment”, web:Prov.6.20) reopens the lecture-frame vocative that reappears here after 6:1. The unit binds the commandment to the body (6:21, tied on the heart, bound on the neck) and to a light-metaphor: "נֵ֣ר מִ֭צְוָה וְת֣וֹרָה א֑וֹר" (oshb:Prov.6.23; “the commandment is a lamp, and the law is light”, web:Prov.6.23), closing on “the way of life” (web:Prov.6.23). That closing figure completes the metaphor opened at 6:20-21 before 6:24 pivots to a purpose clause naming a specific new threat, the adulteress, not yet in view in 6:20-23.
rejected_alternative: Extending this unit through 6:26 was rejected because 6:24 opens an infinitive-of-purpose clause naming a new addressee-threat (the adulteress) that the lamp/light metaphor of 6:20-23 has not yet introduced.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Prov.6.20 vocative "נְצֹ֣ר בְּ֭נִי מִצְוַ֣ת אָבִ֑יךָ" reopening the lecture frame
oshb:Prov.6.21 body-binding imperatives (heart/neck)

device_notes: Synthetic parallelism (metaphor built across four verses); no antithetic pivot. oshb:Prov.6.19, the verse immediately before this unit, closes the numerical saying with its own petuchah in WLC (tier-3 corroboration, single witness); disclosed here as the adjoining mark rather than evidence for the 6:20 vocative-restart argued above. Within 6:20-23 itself the parashah layer stays silent; the next petuchah in sequence sits at 6:26, inside the following unit, so this internal seam rests on the vocative restart and metaphor-closure argued above rather than on parashah corroboration.

rationale: The infinitive-of-purpose clause "לִ֭שְׁמָרְךָ מֵאֵ֣שֶׁת רָ֑ע..." (oshb:Prov.6.24; “to keep you from the immoral woman”, web:Prov.6.24) governs the whole span: it states the aim, 6:25 issues the matching prohibition (do not lust after her beauty), 6:26 supplies the causal warrant (a prostitute reduces you to a loaf of bread), and 6:27-28 supply a paired rhetorical-question analogy (fire in the lap, walking on coals) that 6:29 applies directly back to the purpose clause's subject: "כֵּ֗ן הַ֭בָּא אֶל אֵ֣שֶׁת רֵעֵ֑הוּ..." (oshb:Prov.6.29; “So is he who goes in to his neighbor's wife”, web:Prov.6.29). The unit closes there, before 6:30 opens an unrelated comparison subject, the thief.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the fire-and-coals rhetorical questions (6:27-29) into their own row was rejected because they supply the warrant for the prohibition of 6:24-26 under one governing purpose clause, not an independent topic. The petuchah at 6:26 is disclosed as tier-3 corroboration for a possible 6:20-26/6:27-35 split, but the governing purpose infinitive opened at 6:24 argues against treating 6:26 as the operative seam.

device_notes: Synthetic-to-applied argument structure (purpose, prohibition, warrant, analogy, application); the fire/coals pair in 6:27-28 is the unit's rhetorical-question figure. A petuchah is attested at 6:26 in WLC (tier-3 corroboration, single witness); it falls inside this span rather than at its edge and is disclosed here rather than treated as the boundary driver, per the governing-clause argument above.

rationale: "לֹא יָב֣וּזוּ לַ֭גַּנָּב..." (oshb:Prov.6.30; “Men don't despise a thief...”, web:Prov.6.30) opens a new comparison subject: a thief who steals from hunger draws some social allowance and owes restitution (6:30-31), but the adulterer, unlike the thief, "is void of understanding" and “destroys his own soul” (web:Prov.6.32), facing wounds, dishonor, and a husband's unrelenting jealousy that "will not spare in the day of vengeance" and “won't regard any ransom” (web:Prov.6.34-35). The a fortiori argument (lesser case, thief, versus greater case, adulterer) is confined to these six verses and closes the chapter at the petuchah of 6:35, before the next lecture reopens at 7:1 outside this part.
rejected_alternative: Reading 6:30-35 as a single_proverb was rejected because the thief-versus-adulterer comparison unfolds across paired clauses building one a fortiori argument, not one couplet; treating it as a numerical_saying was also rejected, since no x-of-y count governs the span.

A petuchah closes 6:35 in WLC (tier-3 corroboration, single witness), matching the chapter-end boundary; 6:29 is cited here to mark where the preceding unit's application clause ends, not as evidence internal to this span.
